description: Galaxy X is a San Diego team built around engineering and machine learning. I’m Brian, and I specialize in engineering and programming, especially machine learning. We want to ship a polished, working app for this competition. We need people who can code in Java and Python and have experience making apps.
summary:
We built Skyframe Observatory, an interactive astronomy platform that lets people explore NASA SPHEREx observations and investigate objects that move or change brightness. Users can enter sky coordinates or choose a guided target. We verified that the app retrieves and renders observations for all five challenge fields.

Our design started with one question: How can someone tell whether an apparent change is real? Alignment errors and differences in wavelength or image sharpness can create misleading signals. We used Jupyter notebook experiments to guide image alignment and comparison, then built significance maps showing how strongly changes stand out from estimated noise.

One example of a section, Shift & Stack, allows users to combine four exposures of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS along its predicted path, then reverse the path to see the signal spread out. Users can export observation IDs and processing settings so others can reproduce their analyses. This allows volunteers to share evidence that researchers can independently verify.

Instead of switching between different programs to test ideas, analyze observations, or record findings, users can do everything through one platform. Our goal was to remove barriers between curiosity and scientific investigation, making NASA's astronomical data accessible regardless of experience or technical expertise.
details:
Our project, Skyframe Observatory, is an interactive website that allows anyone to explore real observations from NASA's SPHEREx telescope. Users can explore different areas of the sky, track changes over time, compare images, adjust brightness, and investigate moving or changing objects. The website retrieves data directly from NASA/IPAC's archive, giving users access to real scientific observations.

One of our biggest priorities was accuracy. We realized that just because two images look different doesn't necessarily mean something has changed in space. Differences in wavelength, background noise, and image alignment can create misleading signals. To address this, we developed methods to account for these differences while giving users the ability to examine the underlying measurements themselves.

We also developed Shift & Stack, a feature that aligns multiple observations based on an object's predicted movement. We tested it using real SPHEREx images of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and simulated moving objects to evaluate how effectively it could detect motion.

We built the platform using React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, and SciPy. We also used GitHub for collaboration and Docker for deployment.

Rather than creating a basic tool that simply displays an image when users enter coordinates, we wanted to build a complete platform where people could investigate their own questions. For example, users can explore real SPHEREx observations, compare images from different times to identify changes, and use significance maps to determine whether those changes stand out from background noise. They can also use Shift & Stack to investigate moving objects, adjust image brightness to examine faint details, and record their findings through built-in note-taking tools. They can also examine brightness measurements across different wavelengths to better understand an object's properties and identify unusual patterns. By combining data retrieval, analysis, and documentation in one place, we allow users to carry out their own astronomical investigations without switching between multiple programs.

Ultimately, our goal was to make astronomy more accessible. We wanted to give people the opportunity to explore NASA's data, investigate potential discoveries, and share their findings, regardless of their technical experience.
